Thanks for the walkthrough today, Marissa. A couple of follow-ups from my side after talking with our security team: 

1) What exactly gets logged for a request/response pair? Are headers, trace IDs, and request body stored in full?
2) Can we redact or hash PII (SSNs, account numbers) at the ingestion layer so it never lands in long-term logs?
3) How long are logs retained in hosted vs. dedicated/private deployments? We need to map to our retention policy (30 days for full request, 365 days for metadata).

Also tagging our CISO Maria (cc) and Legal since they may want artifacts (SOC-2 evidence, redaction spec).

Appreciate any specifics you can share so we can move to procurement.

—Alex

Alex — thanks for the notes and for looping Maria/Legal. High level answers below; I'll loop in our engineers for the technical detail and a short redaction spec draft.

• What gets logged: By default our hosted API captures request metadata (timestamps, route, model, latency, token counts), request/response payloads for troubleshooting (text) and select headers (user-agent, request-id). We do not persist raw audio or file binaries unless explicitly uploaded as attachments.

• PII redaction: We support configurable redaction at the ingress layer for hosted/dedicated/private. Options: automatic pattern-based masking (PII regex), custom redaction rules (field names/paths), and a pass-through hashing option so sensitive values are hashed and the original is never stored. For regulated customers we recommend ingress redaction + customer-managed keys for hashing.

• Retention: Hosted default is 90 days for full payloads, 3 years for metadata. For Dedicated/Private we can enforce custom retention windows (e.g., 30 days full, 365 metadata) as part of contract/SLA. Deleted logs can be tombstoned for audit but removed from queryable storage within configured windows.

Next steps: Ill have Dev and Rishi add technical details on headers/trace IDs and share a short redaction_spec.xlsx along with SOC-2 evidence links. Can you confirm the exact fields/patterns your team wants redacted (SSN, 16-digit card numbers, account_id)?

Thanks, Alex/Marissa — adding the technical specifics from the runtime side. TL;DR: we have multiple knobs to avoid sensitive data persisting in logs.

Detailed behavior (hosted default unless overridden):
- Request metadata always logged: request_id, route, model_version, latency_ms, token_counts, client_ip (anonymized), timestamp.
- Headers: we capture a small allowlist by default (user-agent, x-redwood-route, x-request-id). Any header not on the allowlist is dropped at the ingress and not stored. Customers can configure the header allowlist in Dedicated/Private.
- Trace IDs: out-of-band trace IDs (x-trace-id) are stored as part of metadata to enable tracing of requests, but payloads containing the trace id are subject to redaction rules if they match PII patterns.
- Request/response bodies: captured for debugging. We offer three retention/redaction modes: 
   1) None (store as-is)
   2) Masking (pattern-based replace with ****) — performed at ingestion pipeline before storage.
   3) Hashing (HMAC-SHA256 with customer key) — original is never stored.

Redaction specifics:
- Built-in detectors: SSN (US), credit card Luhn + BIN detection, email patterns, ISO8601 timestamps, phone numbers.
- Custom rules: allow regex or JSONPath/field selectors. Rules execute in a configurable order; we recommend running custom rules last to avoid over-masking.

Operational controls:
- Redaction happens in-stream at edge proxies (for hosted) or within the customer VPC (private).
- Masked values are replaced with a stable token so relative comparisons are possible (e.g., <REDACTED:acct_1234>).
- Hashing uses per-customer keys when available; we support KMS/HSM integrations for key management.

Data residency & retention:
- For hosted customers we store logs in region of the account (US/EU/APAC) with configurable retention windows. For Dedicated/Private you control storage and retention policy; we can commit to 30-day payload retention in contract for FIN-regulated customers.

I'm attaching a quick redaction_spec.xlsx that shows sample regexes and example transforms. Let me know if you want us to run a test ingestion with a sanitized sample dataset.

—Dev

This is helpful — thanks Dev. A couple clarifications from our side: 

• We want request/response payloads retained for max 30 days, metadata for 365. That should be configurable for Dedicated.
• Header allowlist: we want to ensure x-correlation-id and x-request-id are retained for tracing, and that auth headers are never stored.
• For hashing we want it to be irreversible and use our own KMS key.

Can you confirm the exact header allowlist you capture by default and whether auth headers (Authorization, Cookie) are explicitly dropped before any ingestion? Also please share the SOC-2 report link and the redaction_spec.xlsx. If everything looks good I'll route this to procurement/legal for contract language.

Subject: Re: Quick demo — logging & redaction questions

Alex — summary and attachments per your asks.

1) Retention: We can do 30 days payload / 365 days metadata for Dedicated and include in SOW.
2) Header allowlist: default allowlist = [User-Agent, X-Request-Id, X-Redwood-Route, X-Correlation-Id]. Authorization, Cookie, and any header matching "Authorization" or "Cookie" are dropped at ingress and never persisted. You can add headers to the allowlist via Dedicated config, but we recommend avoiding auth headers.
3) Hashing: supported and irreversible. We support customer-managed KMS keys (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault). Hashing uses HMAC-SHA256 with salt and KMS sign where available.

Attached: security_questionnaire_v2.pdf, redaction_spec.xlsx. SOC-2 Type II report: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1A2b3C-redaction-specs (shared).

Next step: Alex, if you approve, I'll share a short mutual action plan and loop our contracting team to lock retention clauses into the Dedicated offer. If Legal wants additional attestations (e.g., pen test, data-flow diagram) we can provide those as well.

Thanks — Marissa
